name: Caffeine avoidance

lead: Caffeine avoidance means cutting out coffee, tea and energy drinks, in appearance communities often to reduce facial puffiness and improve sleep, which people link to a fresher look.

Caffeine is a stimulant that blocks adenosine receptors and can delay or prevent sleep. Large acute doses of about 250 to 300 mg temporarily increase urine output mainly in people who have abstained, while regular users develop tolerance. No published study has tested caffeine avoidance for facial puffiness.

paras: People stop drinking coffee and energy drinks, or taper down, and switch to decaf or herbal tea. Some set a caffeine cutoff earlier in the day instead of quitting entirely.
Quitting can cause withdrawal symptoms such as headache and fatigue, commonly for a day or so.

angle.text: Users cut caffeine hoping for better sleep and less facial puffiness, which they link to a fresher look. Caffeine is documented to disrupt sleep; its effect on puffiness has not been tested.

lead: Caffeine avoidance is cutting out coffee, tea and energy drinks, in appearance communities often for the stated aim of reducing facial puffiness and improving sleep.

Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant that can delay or prevent sleep, and large acute doses of about 250 to 300 mg temporarily increase urine output mainly in people who have abstained, while regular users develop tolerance.[1] No published study was found testing caffeine avoidance for facial puffiness.

paras: Around 100 mg a day may disrupt sleep in some regular users, though others develop tolerance.[1] The diuretic effect appears in abstainers and fades with regular use, so the dehydration risk is limited to acute large doses.[1]
Withdrawal affects about 11% by self-report, typically lasting no more than a day at lower intakes, with headache, fatigue and low mood among the symptoms.[1]

Health Canada and EFSA give 400 mg a day as a limit for healthy adults and 200 to 300 mg for pregnancy, depending on the agency.[1] A 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intakes.[2]
Practitioners link caffeine to puffiness and poor sleep. The sources reviewed do not discuss skin or puffiness effects of caffeine.
No studies found on caffeine avoidance and facial puffiness.
